With regard to the origin of Sangita, we are quite in the dark. i
In the absence of historic light, all our attempts to penetrate the thick

gloom of antiquity prove abortive. The accounts of ancient India are

either buried in the abyss of time, or so enveloped in mythical legends
that they appear to us too obscure to reason upon. ‘The accounts of the
Purinas or later religious books of the Ilindus, are so wrapped up in mys-
teries and fables that we can hardly confide in their veracity. It was a
very common custom with the ancients to ascribe to divine revelation the

invention of all the arts and the sciences of which they possessed no records.

‘Lhe human voice is distinguished according to its gramasthana, or tire

Srutis form’ the eround-work on which the superstructure of
{Tindu music is built. All attempts te comprehend its principles without

intend to give a clear exposition of the nature of srutis and. their

Srutis, in the musical acceptation of the term, are particles of sound,
perceivable by the ear. They are the essential elements in the formation
of the tones of which sapdaka or octave is composed. They vary in qua-
lity or intensity according to the places of their origin; véz., the chest, the
throat, and the head; those of the throat vibrating twice as rapidly, and,

being consequently twice as intense, as these similar ones of the chest;

We learn from the Saiskrita writers that the vatioiis gradations of

Men generally question the truth of this statement which, in their
